Entries that existed before their type joined the workflow are at the first stage.

When you change a workflow later:

* Removing a stage sends its entries back to the first stage.
* Removing a content type from the workflow clears the stages of its entries.
* Deleting the workflow clears the stages and assignees of its entries.

## Move and assign entries

[Section titled “Move and assign entries”](#move-and-assign-entries)

The entry editor shows a **Review** panel with the **Stage** and the **Assignee**.

* Pick another **Stage** to move the entry. Stages reserved for other roles cannot be chosen, and the panel says so. Admins with **Manage review workflows** can always move entries.
* Pick an **Assignee** from the active admins who can read the content type, or select **Remove assignee**. Anyone who can update the entry can assign it.
* When the workflow has a required stage, the panel says which stage the entry must reach before **Publish** works.

The list view shows a **Stage** column, and the home page lists the entries assigned to you under **Assigned to me**. Localized types keep a stage per locale.

## What the publish stage blocks

[Section titled “What the publish stage blocks”](#what-the-publish-stage-blocks)

The required stage applies to every way of publishing: the admin panel, REST, GraphQL, releases and plugins. A publication of an entry outside that stage fails with `400`:

```text
the entry must be in the review stage `Ready` to be published
```

In Strapi the stage requirement applies only to the admin panel. Stage roles also differ: in Verdin they limit who moves entries *into* a stage.

## Audit logs and webhooks

[Section titled “Audit logs and webhooks”](#audit-logs-and-webhooks)

* Stage changes and assignments are recorded in the [audit logs](/verdin/guides/content/audit-logs/) as `entry.stage` and `entry.assign`.
* Webhooks can subscribe to **Entry stage changed** (`review-workflows.updateEntryStage`). See [Webhooks](/verdin/guides/integrations/webhooks/).

## Admin API

[Section titled “Admin API”](#admin-api)

All routes are under `/admin/api` and take an admin access token.

| Route                                                  | Permission         | Does                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `GET /review-workflows`, `GET /review-workflows/{id}`  | `workflows.manage` | Workflows with their stages.                                                                              |
| `POST /review-workflows`, `PUT /review-workflows/{id}` | `workflows.manage` | Create or replace a workflow (body below).                                                                |
| `DELETE /review-workflows/{id}`                        | `workflows.manage` | Entries of its types lose their stages.                                                                   |
| `GET /content/{uid}/{documentId}/review?locale=`       | read the entry     | Stage, assignee, and the stages you can move the entry to (`canMoveTo`).                                  |
| `PUT /content/{uid}/{documentId}/review?locale=`       | update the entry   | `{ "stageId": 3, "assigneeId": 7 }`. Both fields are optional; `"assigneeId": null` removes the assignee. |
| `GET /content/{uid}/review?documentIds=a,b`            | read the type      | Stages of up to 200 entries, with the workflow in `meta.workflow`.                                        |
| `GET /review/assigned`                                 | signed in          | Entries assigned to you.                                                                                  |
| `GET /review/assignees?uid=`                           | update the type    | Active admins who can read the type.                                                                      |
| `GET /review/roles`                                    | `workflows.manage` | Role codes and names, for stage roles.                                                                    |

A workflow as sent to `POST` and `PUT`:

```json
{
  "name": "Editorial",
  "contentTypes": ["api::article"],
  "stages": [
    { "id": 1, "name": "To do", "color": "#4945ff" },
    { "id": 2, "name": "In review", "color": "#ff8800" },
    { "name": "Ready", "color": "#2f9e44", "roles": ["editor"] }
  ],
  "publishStage": "Ready"
}
```

* A workflow has 1 to 50 stages with unique names and `#rrggbb` colors.
* `publishStage` names one of the stages; leave it out for none.
* Send existing stages with their `id` so their entries stay where they are. Stages without an `id` are new.

Note

Turning the feature off hides the stages and stops enforcing the publish stage. The workflows and entry stages are kept for when you turn it back on.

# Search

> Search entries with _q, and turn on the Tantivy full-text index for ranked, accent-insensitive results.

The content API and the admin panel search entries with the `_q` parameter, as in Strapi. By default `_q` matches text fields that contain the words. Turn on the `[search]` index to rank results with a full-text engine (Tantivy) built into the server. This guide shows both and when to use the index.

## Search with `_q`

[Section titled “Search with \_q”](#search-with-_q)

Terminal

```sh
curl -G 'http://localhost:1337/api/articles' --data-urlencode '_q=rust cms'
```

`_q` combines with the other parameters: `filters`, `status`, `locale`, `pagination`, `fields` and `populate`. The search box of the admin list sends the same parameter.

Which fields are searched:

* Text fields: `string`, `text`, `richtext`, `email`, `uid` and `enumeration`.
* With the index, also the text inside `blocks`, components and dynamic zones.
* Never private fields or passwords.

`_q` is a REST parameter. GraphQL and the TypeScript client’s query options have no search argument; use a `$containsi` filter there.

## Without the index

[Section titled “Without the index”](#without-the-index)

Without `[search]`, `_q` matches entries where any text field contains the whole search text, ignoring case, like Strapi’s `$containsi`. Results follow the usual sort. This needs no setup and works on every database, but it scans the table and does not rank.

## Turn on the full-text index

[Section titled “Turn on the full-text index”](#turn-on-the-full-text-index)

1. Enable the index in `verdin.toml`:

   verdin.toml

   ```toml
   [search]
   enabled = true
   ```

2. Restart Verdin. It builds the index in the background from every entry; until it is ready, `_q` falls back to `$containsi`.

| Key         | Default         | Description                               |
| ----------- | --------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`   | `false`         | Rank `_q` with the full-text index.       |
| `dir`       | `"data/search"` | Index directory, relative to the project. |
| `memory_mb` | `50`            | Indexing memory budget, in megabytes.     |

See the [configuration reference](/verdin/reference/configuration/).

How the index matches:

* Words are split on anything that is not a letter or digit, lowercased and stripped of accents, so `cafe` finds `Café`.
* Every word must match. The last word also matches as a prefix, so results appear while someone types.
* The title (the type’s first text field) weighs double.
* Without a `sort`, results come best match first. With a `sort`, the matches are sorted your way. At most 1,000 matches are considered per search.
* Drafts and published versions, and each locale, are searched separately, following `status` and `locale`.

The index follows every write from any API. It is rebuilt when the schema changes the searchable fields, and when its directory is missing.

## Several instances

[Section titled “Several instances”](#several-instances)

The index lives on the instance’s disk and follows that instance’s writes. When you run several instances, writes on one do not reach the index of the others. Keep search on a single instance, or rebuild after a deploy by deleting the index directory before the start. See [Scaling](/verdin/deploy/scaling/).

Tip

The index directory is safe to delete. Keep it out of backups and version control; Verdin rebuilds it from the database.

# Forms

> Define contact and sign-up forms in the admin panel, post to them from your site, and read or export the submissions.

The **Forms** feature handles the forms of your site (contact, newsletter sign-up, event registration) without a form service. Editors define the fields in the admin panel, your site renders them and posts to Verdin, and submissions are validated, stored, emailed and exported as CSV.

## Turn it on

[Section titled “Turn it on”](#turn-it-on)

In **Settings → Features**, turn on **Forms**, then choose **Manage forms** (or go to **Settings → Forms**). Managing forms and reading submissions needs the **Manage SEO, redirects, menus and forms** permission (`site.manage`), which the built-in Editor role has. See [Permissions](/verdin/reference/permissions/).

For notification emails, configure a provider in [`[email]`](/verdin/reference/configuration/); with the default `log` provider, emails are only written to the server log.

## Create a form

[Section titled “Create a form”](#create-a-form)

1. In **Settings → Forms**, choose **New form**.

2. Give it a name (such as **Contact**) and a **Slug** (`contact`). The slug is part of the form’s URL.

3. On the **Fields** tab, choose **Add a field** for each field, with its **Label**, **Name**, **Type**, **Required**, **Placeholder** and **Maximum length**.

4. On the **Settings** tab, set:

   * **Notify**: email addresses that receive every submission.
   * **Success message**: returned to your site after a submission.
   * **Spam trap**: on by default (see [Spam](#spam)).

5. Save. The **Integration** tab shows the public endpoint and an example to copy.

| Type       | Label in the admin | Accepts                                                                                           |
| ---------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `text`     | **Text**           | Any text.                                                                                         |
| `email`    | **Email**          | An email address.                                                                                 |
| `textarea` | **Long text**      | Any text.                                                                                         |
| `number`   | **Number**         | A number, stored as a number.                                                                     |
| `select`   | **Choice**         | One of its **Options** (one per line).                                                            |
| `checkbox` | **Checkbox**       | `true`, `on`, `1` or `yes` is checked; anything else is not. A required checkbox must be checked. |
| `date`     | **Date**           | Any text (use `<input type="date">`).                                                             |
| `url`      | **URL**            | A URL.                                                                                            |
| `tel`      | **Phone**          | Any text.                                                                                         |

Field names start with a letter, then letters, digits or `_`, and are unique in the form. A form has 1 to 50 fields. Values are at most **Maximum length** characters (5,000 by default, 20,000 at most).

## Render the form

[Section titled “Render the form”](#render-the-form)

`GET /api/_forms/{slug}` returns the definition, so your site can render the fields the editors chose:

```json
{
  "data": {
    "slug": "contact",
    "name": "Contact",
    "fields": [
      { "name": "email", "label": "Email", "type": "email", "required": true },
      { "name": "message", "label": "Message", "type": "textarea", "required": true, "maxLength": 2000 },
      { "name": "topic", "label": "Topic", "type": "select", "options": ["Sales", "Support"] }
    ],
    "honeypot": "_gotcha"
  }
}
```

`honeypot` is `null` when the spam trap is off. The definition is cached for a minute (`Cache-Control: public, max-age=60`).

## Submit

[Section titled “Submit”](#submit)

`POST /api/_forms/{slug}` takes the values as JSON (the fields, or `{ "data": { … } }`) or as a plain form post (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`). No token is needed.

* HTML form

  ```html
  <form method="post" action="https://cms.example.com/api/_forms/contact">
    <input name="email" type="email" required />
    <textarea name="message" required maxlength="2000"></textarea>
    <input name="_gotcha" tabindex="-1" autocomplete="off" aria-hidden="true" style="position:absolute;left:-9999px" />
    <button>Send</button>
  </form>
  ```

* fetch

  ```js
  const response = await fetch('https://cms.example.com/api/_forms/contact', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ data: { email, message, _gotcha: '' } }),
  });
  const body = await response.json();
  if (response.ok) showThanks(body.data.message);
  else showErrors(body.error.details.errors); // [{ path: ['email'], message: 'must be an email address' }]
  ```

| Answer                                    | When                                                                                 |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `201` with `{ "data": { "message": … } }` | Accepted. `message` is the **Success message**, or `Thank you!`.                     |
| `400` `ValidationError`                   | A value is missing or invalid. `details.errors` lists `{ path, message }` per field. |
| `404`                                     | No form with that slug, or the feature is off.                                       |
| `413`                                     | The submission is over 64 KB.                                                        |
| `429`                                     | The same visitor sent more than 10 submissions to this form in a minute.             |

Values are trimmed and checked against the fields. Unknown fields are dropped, so a visitor cannot add data you did not ask for.

A plain HTML form post receives the JSON answer as the page. For a better experience, submit with `fetch` and show the message yourself. Posting from the browser to another origin needs your site’s origin in [`[api].cors_origins`](/verdin/reference/configuration/).

### Spam

[Section titled “Spam”](#spam)

With **Spam trap** on, add a hidden, empty `_gotcha` field to the form. Bots fill every field; a submission with `_gotcha` filled is answered as accepted (`201`) and thrown away, so the bot learns nothing. Together with the rate limit, this stops most form spam without a CAPTCHA.

## Read submissions

[Section titled “Read submissions”](#read-submissions)

The form’s **Submissions** tab lists what visitors sent, with the time it was **Received**. You can delete a submission, and **Export CSV** downloads them all.

Every accepted submission is also emailed to the **Notify** addresses, with a link to the submissions in the admin (built from [`[server].public_url`](/verdin/reference/configuration/)).

Note

Verdin stores each submission’s values, the visitor’s user agent, and a keyed hash of their IP address (not the address itself), enough to spot a flood without tracking people. Deleting a form deletes its submissions.

## Admin API

[Section titled “Admin API”](#admin-api)

The admin panel uses `/admin/api/site/forms` and `/admin/api/site/forms/{id}`, plus `/admin/api/site/forms/{id}/submissions` and `…/submissions/export` (CSV), with an admin’s access token and `site.manage`. See [Admin API](/verdin/api/admin/).

# Responsive images

> Serve images at the right size, with the formats Verdin generates on upload and on-the-fly transformations by URL.

Verdin gives you two ways to serve an image at the size a page needs:

* **Responsive formats**, generated once when the image is uploaded (`thumbnail`, `small`, `medium`, `large`), exactly like Strapi’s upload plugin. They work with every upload provider.
* **Transformations**, rendered on request from URL parameters (`?preset=thumb`, or `?w=800&format=webp` with a signature) and cached on disk. They work with the local provider.

Both are part of the media library, which is always on. For uploading and organizing files, see [Media](/verdin/concepts/media/).

## Responsive formats

[Section titled “Responsive formats”](#responsive-formats)

When a JPEG, PNG, WebP, TIFF or BMP image is uploaded, Verdin writes smaller copies of it and lists them in the file’s `formats`:

| Format      | Size                      |
| ----------- | ------------------------- |
| `thumbnail` | Fits in 245 × 156 pixels. |
| `large`     | 1000 pixels wide.         |
| `medium`    | 750 pixels wide.          |
| `small`     | 500 pixels wide.          |

A format is skipped when the image is already smaller, so a 600 pixel wide image only gets `thumbnail` and `small`. Copies keep the original’s format (JPEGs are encoded at quality 80) and its EXIF orientation. GIFs are left alone, because they may be animated.

Populate the media field to get them. The examples use a `cover` media attribute on Article; the example blog has none, so add one in the content-type builder to follow along.

* REST

  Terminal

  ```sh
  curl -g 'https://cms.example.com/api/articles?populate[cover]=true'
  ```

* GraphQL

  ```graphql
  query {
    articles {
      title
      cover { url width height alternativeText formats }
    }
  }
  ```

* TypeScript

  ```ts
  const { data } = await verdin.collection('articles').find({ populate: { cover: true } });
  const formats = data[0].cover?.formats; // Record<string, MediaFormat> | null
  ```

```json
"cover": {
  "url": "/uploads/team_4f1c2a.jpg",
  "width": 2400,
  "height": 1600,
  "alternativeText": "The team at the office",
  "formats": {
    "thumbnail": { "url": "/uploads/thumbnail_team_4f1c2a.jpg", "width": 234, "height": 156 },
    "large": { "url": "/uploads/large_team_4f1c2a.jpg", "width": 1000, "height": 667 },
    "medium": { "url": "/uploads/medium_team_4f1c2a.jpg", "width": 750, "height": 500 },
    "small": { "url": "/uploads/small_team_4f1c2a.jpg", "width": 500, "height": 333 }
  }
}
```

Build a `srcset` from them. With the local provider, `url`s are paths on the Verdin host; prefix them with its origin:

```ts
const CMS = 'https://cms.example.com';


function srcset(image: Media): string {
  const sources = Object.values(image.formats ?? {}).map((f) => `${CMS}${f.url} ${f.width}w`);
  return [...sources, `${CMS}${image.url} ${image.width}w`].join(', ');
}
```

```html
<img src="…/uploads/large_team_4f1c2a.jpg" srcset="…" sizes="(min-width: 60rem) 50vw, 100vw"
     width="2400" height="1600" alt="The team at the office" />
```

### Change the formats

[Section titled “Change the formats”](#change-the-formats)

The formats come from `[upload]` in `verdin.toml`:

verdin.toml

```toml
[upload]
breakpoints = [{ name = "large", width = 1600 }, { name = "small", width = 640 }]
# responsive_formats = false  # no copies at all
# max_original_size = 3000    # scale larger originals down on upload (drops EXIF and GPS)
```

`breakpoints` is Strapi’s setting of the same name. Changes apply to new uploads; existing files keep the formats they have. See [`[upload]`](/verdin/reference/configuration/) for every key, including `max_image_megapixels`, the decoding limit that protects against decompression bombs (100 megapixels by default).

## Transformations

[Section titled “Transformations”](#transformations)

With the local provider, Verdin serves `/uploads/<file>` itself and can render other sizes and formats of an image on request:

```plaintext
/uploads/team_4f1c2a.jpg?preset=thumb
/uploads/team_4f1c2a.jpg?w=800&format=webp&s=<signature>
```

| Parameter | Values                                                                                                                                                                           |
| --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `w`, `h`  | Width and height in pixels, from 1 to `max_size` (4096 by default). With only one, the other follows the aspect ratio. With neither, the image keeps its size (a format change). |
| `fit`     | `cover` (the default) fills the box and crops the rest, keeping the file’s focal point in view. `inside` fits the image within the box. `fill` stretches it to the box.          |
| `format`  | `jpeg` (or `jpg`), `png` or `webp`. WebP output is lossless. Without it the image keeps its format (TIFF and BMP become JPEG).                                                   |
| `q`       | JPEG quality, from 1 to 100. Defaults to 80.                                                                                                                                     |
| `preset`  | A named transformation from the configuration. It cannot be combined with the other parameters.                                                                                  |
| `s`       | The signature, when the parameters are not a preset.                                                                                                                             |

Images are never enlarged: a 600 pixel wide image asked for at `w=1200` comes back at 600. Transformations work on JPEG, PNG, WebP, TIFF and BMP files, not on GIFs.

### Focal point

[Section titled “Focal point”](#focal-point)

Editors set the focal point of an image in the media library: open the file and click the image (**Focal point: click the image or use the arrow keys to set it**). `fit=cover` crops keep that point in view, and changing it drops the cached renderings of the file.

### Presets

[Section titled “Presets”](#presets)

Presets are the transformations you allow anyone to request. Define them in `[upload.transforms.presets]`:

verdin.toml

```toml
[upload.transforms.presets]
thumb = { w = 300, h = 300 }
card = { w = 640, h = 360, format = "webp" }
hero = { w = 1600, h = 600, fit = "cover", format = "jpeg", q = 85 }
```

```html
<img src="https://cms.example.com/uploads/team_4f1c2a.jpg?preset=card" alt="…" />
```

An unknown preset answers `400`.

### Signed parameters

[Section titled “Signed parameters”](#signed-parameters)

Any other combination of `w`, `h`, `fit`, `format` and `q` needs a signature, so nobody can make the server render (and store) an unbounded number of variants. Set a secret in the environment of the server and of the code that builds image URLs:

Terminal

```sh
export VERDIN_IMAGE_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
```

The signature `s` is the hex HMAC-SHA256, keyed with that secret, of `<file>?<canonical query>`. The canonical query lists the parameters you set, except `fit=cover` (the default), sorted by name (`fit`, `format`, `h`, `q`, `w`), with `jpeg` for JPEG:

src/image-url.ts

```ts
import { createHmac } from 'node:crypto';


type Transform = { w?: number; h?: number; fit?: 'cover' | 'inside' | 'fill'; format?: 'jpeg' | 'png' | 'webp'; q?: number };


export function imageUrl(cms: string, url: string, t: Transform): string {
  const file = url.replace(/^\/uploads\//, '');
  const params: [string, string][] = [];
  if (t.fit && t.fit !== 'cover') params.push(['fit', t.fit]);
  if (t.format) params.push(['format', t.format]);
  if (t.h) params.push(['h', String(t.h)]);
  if (t.q) params.push(['q', String(t.q)]);
  if (t.w) params.push(['w', String(t.w)]);
  const query = params.map(([k, v]) => `${k}=${v}`).join('&');
  const s = createHmac('sha256', process.env.VERDIN_IMAGE_SECRET!).update(`${file}?${query}`).digest('hex');
  return `${cms}/uploads/${file}?${query}&s=${s}`;
}
```

Build these URLs on the server (or at build time): the secret must not reach the browser. Without `VERDIN_IMAGE_SECRET`, or with a wrong signature, the request answers `403`.

Caution

`[upload.transforms].allow_arbitrary = true` accepts any parameters without a signature. Every distinct URL is then rendered and cached, so anyone can fill the disk and use the CPU. Only turn it on when the server is reachable from trusted networks alone.

### Caching and limits

[Section titled “Caching and limits”](#caching-and-limits)

* Renderings are written to `[upload.transforms].cache_dir` (`.cache/transforms` by default) and served from there afterwards. The directory is safe to delete.
* Replacing a file or moving its focal point drops its cached renderings.
* Transformed responses are cached by browsers and CDNs for a day (`Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400`); plain files for a year, since their names never change.
* Renders run in parallel up to the number of CPU cores; more requests wait.
* Images larger than `max_image_megapixels` are refused (`422`).

Set `[upload.transforms].enabled = false` to turn transformations off. See [`[upload.transforms]`](/verdin/reference/configuration/) for the keys.

### With S3 and other providers

[Section titled “With S3 and other providers”](#with-s3-and-other-providers)

With the S3 provider, files are served by the bucket or its CDN, not by Verdin, so the transformation parameters do nothing. Use the responsive formats, or the image service of your CDN (for example Cloudflare Images or imgix) in front of the bucket’s `public_url`.

Strapi has no built-in transformations; its responsive formats and `breakpoints` behave the same as Verdin’s.

# Menus

> Build navigation menus of links and entries in the admin panel and render them on your site.

The **Menus** feature gives editors named navigation trees (a header, a footer, a sidebar) that link to pages, entries or other sites. Your site fetches a menu by its slug and renders it; links to entries follow their published state and path.

In Strapi this usually takes a navigation plugin or a hand-made menu content type; in Verdin it is built in.

## Turn it on

[Section titled “Turn it on”](#turn-it-on)

In **Settings → Features**, turn on **Menus**, then choose **Manage menus** (or go to **Settings → Menus**). Managing menus needs the **Manage SEO, redirects, menus and forms** permission (`site.manage`), which the built-in Editor role has. See [Permissions](/verdin/reference/permissions/).

To link entries by path, also set up path patterns in [SEO and sitemap](/verdin/guides/frontend/seo-and-sitemap/).

## Build a menu

[Section titled “Build a menu”](#build-a-menu)

1. In **Settings → Menus**, choose **New menu**.

2. Give it a name (such as **Main navigation**) and a **Slug** (`main`): lowercase letters, digits and dashes. Sites fetch the menu by its slug.

3. Choose **Add an item** and fill in the item:

   * **Label**: the text of the link, up to 255 characters.
   * **Links to**: **A URL**, **An entry**, or **Nothing (a heading)**.
   * **URL**: a path (`/about`), an anchor (`#team`), or an `http(s)`, `mailto:` or `tel:` link.
   * For an entry, choose **Choose an entry**: pick the **Content type** if several can be linked, search the entries and select one.
   * **Opens in**: **The same tab** or **A new tab**.

4. Drag items to order and nest them, or use their buttons. With the keyboard, on a drag handle: Alt+↑ and Alt+↓ move an item, Alt+→ nests it under the one above, Alt+← moves it out.

5. Save.

A menu has at most 5 levels and 500 items.

## Fetch a menu

[Section titled “Fetch a menu”](#fetch-a-menu)

Sites read a menu from `GET /api/_menus/{slug}`, with no token. Add `?locale=` for localized content:

Terminal

```sh
curl 'https://cms.example.com/api/_menus/main?locale=fr'
```

```json
{
  "data": {
    "slug": "main",
    "name": "Main navigation",
    "items": [
      { "id": "a1", "label": "Blog", "url": "/blog" },
      {
        "id": "a2",
        "label": "Topics",
        "children": [
          {
            "id": "a3",
            "label": "Rust",
            "entry": { "uid": "api::category", "documentId": "hx2n8r3w…", "path": "/fr/topics/rust" },
            "url": "/fr/topics/rust"
          }
        ]
      },
      { "id": "a4", "label": "Contact", "url": "mailto:hello@example.com", "target": "_blank" }
    ]
  }
}
```

How entry links resolve:

* An entry that is not published, in the requested locale, is left out of the menu (with its children). Menus never leak drafts.
* `entry.path` comes from the type’s pattern in [SEO and sitemap](/verdin/guides/frontend/seo-and-sitemap/), filled with the entry’s fields and the locale. It is `null` when the type has no pattern or the entry does not fill it.
* When the item has no `url` of its own, it gets the path as `url`, so most sites only need to read `url`.

Without `locale`, entries are read in the default locale. The response is sent with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60`.

## Render it

[Section titled “Render it”](#render-it)

Nav.tsx

```tsx
type Item = { label: string; url?: string; target?: '_self' | '_blank'; children?: Item[] };


export async function Nav({ locale }: { locale: string }) {
  const response = await fetch(`${process.env.VERDIN_URL}/api/_menus/main?locale=${locale}`);
  const { data } = await response.json();
  return <ul>{data.items.map((item: Item) => <NavItem key={item.label} item={item} />)}</ul>;
}


function NavItem({ item }: { item: Item }) {
  return (
    <li>
      {item.url ? <a href={item.url} target={item.target}>{item.label}</a> : <span>{item.label}</span>}
      {item.children?.length ? <ul>{item.children.map((child) => <NavItem key={child.label} item={child} />)}</ul> : null}
    </li>
  );
}
```

Note

Deleting a menu makes `/api/_menus/{slug}` answer `404`, as does turning the feature off. Handle that on your site, for example by rendering no navigation.

## Admin API

[Section titled “Admin API”](#admin-api)

The admin panel uses `/admin/api/site/menus` (`GET`, `POST`) and `/admin/api/site/menus/{id}` (`GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`), with an admin’s access token and `site.manage`. See [Admin API](/verdin/api/admin/).

# Realtime updates

> Refresh your frontend the moment content changes, by subscribing to Verdin's server-sent events.

With the **Realtime** feature on, Verdin streams a small event each time an entry or a media file changes. A frontend subscribes to the stream and refetches what changed: a live blog, a scoreboard, a dashboard that never needs a reload. Each subscriber only receives events about content it may read.

This page shows how to use the stream from a frontend. The event names, payloads and rules are in the [realtime API reference](/verdin/api/realtime/). Strapi v5 has no built-in equivalent.

## Turn it on

[Section titled “Turn it on”](#turn-it-on)

1. In **Settings → Features**, turn on **Realtime**.

2. Decide who subscribes. The stream uses the content API’s permissions:

   * for anyone, allow **Find** or **Find one** on the types in **Settings → Public access**;
   * for a server or an app, create an [API token](/verdin/guides/auth/api-tokens/) with those permissions (and **Read drafts** to receive draft-only events);
   * for signed-in end users, their JWT works too (see [End users](/verdin/guides/auth/end-users/)).

The stream is `GET /api/_events`. Add `?types=` with a comma-separated list of content type uids to receive only those (`plugin::upload` is the media library):

Terminal

```sh
curl -N "https://cms.example.com/api/_events?types=api::article,api::category"
```

```plaintext
event: ready
data: {}


event: entry.publish
data: {"event":"entry.publish","uid":"api::article","documentId":"01j9…","locale":"en"}
```

## Subscribe from a browser

[Section titled “Subscribe from a browser”](#subscribe-from-a-browser)

Events carry ids, not content. On each event, refetch what you show, through the same API and permissions as any other read.

* Public

  With the public role, the browser’s `EventSource` is enough, and it reconnects by itself:

  ```js
  const CMS = 'https://cms.example.com';
  const events = new EventSource(`${CMS}/api/_events?types=api::article`);


  for (const name of ['entry.publish', 'entry.unpublish', 'entry.delete']) {
    events.addEventListener(name, (event) => {
      const { documentId } = JSON.parse(event.data);
      refreshArticle(documentId);
    });
  }


  events.addEventListener('lagged', () => refreshEverything());
  ```

* With a token

  `EventSource` cannot send an `Authorization` header. Read the stream with `fetch` instead, and reconnect when it ends:

  ```js
  async function subscribe(token, onEvent) {
    for (;;) {
      try {
        const response = await fetch(`${CMS}/api/_events?types=api::article`, {
          headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
        });
        if (response.status === 401 || response.status === 403) return; // token refused
        const reader = response.body.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream()).getReader();
        let buffer = '';
        for (;;) {
          const { value, done } = await reader.read();
          if (done) break;
          buffer += value;
          let end;
          while ((end = buffer.indexOf('\n\n')) >= 0) {
            const block = buffer.slice(0, end);
            buffer = buffer.slice(end + 2);
            const name = block.match(/^event: (.*)$/m)?.[1];
            const data = block.match(/^data: (.*)$/m)?.[1];
            if (name && data) onEvent(name, JSON.parse(data));
          }
        }
      } catch {
        // network error: retry below
      }
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 2000));
    }
  }
  ```

  Any SSE client library that supports headers works as well.

Caution

A token in browser code is readable by anyone who opens the page. Only ship a read-only token scoped to the types the page shows, or subscribe from your server and forward the updates to the browser.

Calling the stream from a site on another origin needs that origin in [`[api].cors_origins`](/verdin/reference/configuration/).

## Keep the stream healthy

[Section titled “Keep the stream healthy”](#keep-the-stream-healthy)

* The first event is `ready`: the subscription is live.
* A stream ends after an hour. Reconnect then: `EventSource` does it automatically, and reconnecting also checks the token again, so a revoked token stops receiving events.
* An event named `lagged` means the client read too slowly and missed events. Refetch everything the page shows.
* Draft-only events (`entry.create`, `entry.update` and `entry.discard-draft` on draft & publish types) only reach callers with **Read drafts**. A public site typically listens to `entry.publish`, `entry.unpublish` and `entry.delete`.

## Behind a load balancer

[Section titled “Behind a load balancer”](#behind-a-load-balancer)

With several instances, turn on the shared event bus (`[cluster].bus = "database"`): a client connected to any instance then receives the events of all of them. Without it, events are those of the instance a client is connected to; use sticky sessions for `/api/_events`, or point realtime clients at a single instance. See [Scaling](/verdin/deploy/scaling/#shared-event-bus).

The admin panel uses its own stream (`/admin/api/events`) for live updates, presence and soft locks while editing; see the [realtime API reference](/verdin/api/realtime/).

# Redirects

> Keep a list of redirects in the admin panel and apply them in your site's middleware.

The **Redirects** feature lets editors send old paths to new ones without a deploy: they keep the list in the admin panel, and your site fetches it and answers with the redirect. Verdin does not redirect visitors itself, since they reach your site, not the CMS.

## Turn it on

[Section titled “Turn it on”](#turn-it-on)

In **Settings → Features**, turn on **Redirects**, then choose **Manage redirects** (or go to **Settings → Redirects**). Managing redirects needs the **Manage SEO, redirects, menus and forms** permission (`site.manage`), which the built-in Editor role has. See [Permissions](/verdin/reference/permissions/).

## Add redirects

[Section titled “Add redirects”](#add-redirects)

1. In **Settings → Redirects**, choose **Add a redirect**.
2. **From**: the old path, starting with `/` (for example `/blog/2024/hello`).
3. **To**: the new path, or a full `http(s)` URL on another site.
4. **Type**: **301 · Permanent**, **302 · Temporary**, **307 · Temporary (keeps method)** or **308 · Permanent (keeps method)**.
5. Save.

Verdin refuses a redirect that would never work:

* a second redirect from the same path;
* a path that redirects to itself;
* a chain that loops (`/a` → `/b` → `/a`).

For many redirects at once, use **Import CSV** with `source`, `destination` and `status` columns. Rows whose source already exists update that redirect. **Export CSV** writes the same format, handy for a migration from another CMS or a spreadsheet review.

redirects.csv

```csv
source,destination,status
/blog/2024/hello,/blog/hello,301
/old-pricing,https://shop.example.com/pricing,302
```

## Apply them on your site

[Section titled “Apply them on your site”](#apply-them-on-your-site)

Sites read the list from `GET /api/_redirects`, with no token:

```json
{
  "data": [
    { "source": "/blog/2024/hello", "destination": "/blog/hello", "status": 301 },
    { "source": "/old-pricing", "destination": "https://shop.example.com/pricing", "status": 302 }
  ]
}
```

The response is sent with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60`, so a change reaches sites within about a minute. Match the request path exactly against `source`:

* Next.js

  middleware.js

  ```js
  import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';


  export async function middleware(request) {
    const response = await fetch(`${process.env.VERDIN_URL}/api/_redirects`, { next: { revalidate: 60 } });
    const { data } = await response.json();
    const hit = data.find((redirect) => redirect.source === request.nextUrl.pathname);
    if (hit) return NextResponse.redirect(new URL(hit.destination, request.url), hit.status);
  }
  ```

* Astro

  src/middleware.ts

  ```ts
  import { defineMiddleware } from 'astro:middleware';


  let cache: { at: number; list: { source: string; destination: string; status: number }[] } | null = null;


  export const onRequest = defineMiddleware(async (context, next) => {
    if (!cache || Date.now() - cache.at > 60_000) {
      const response = await fetch(`${import.meta.env.VERDIN_URL}/api/_redirects`);
      cache = { at: Date.now(), list: (await response.json()).data };
    }
    const hit = cache.list.find((redirect) => redirect.source === context.url.pathname);
    if (hit) return context.redirect(hit.destination, hit.status as 301 | 302 | 307 | 308);
    return next();
  });
  ```

For a static site, fetch the list at build time and write your host’s redirect file (Netlify’s `_redirects`, Vercel’s `vercel.json`, an nginx map). Combine that with a [deploy button](/verdin/guides/integrations/deploys-and-cdn/) or a [webhook](/verdin/guides/integrations/webhooks/) so editors can rebuild after changing redirects.

Note

The API prefix follows [`[api].prefix`](/verdin/reference/configuration/). With the feature off, `/api/_redirects` answers `404`.

## Admin API

[Section titled “Admin API”](#admin-api)

The admin panel uses `/admin/api/site/redirects` (`GET`, `POST`) and `/admin/api/site/redirects/{id}` (`PUT`, `DELETE`), with an admin’s access token and `site.manage`. The list is paged and takes `search` (see [Lists](/verdin/api/admin/#lists)).

# SEO and sitemap

> Map content types to the paths of your site, serve a sitemap.xml of every published entry, and add a standard SEO component.

The **SEO and sitemap** feature tells Verdin where each entry lives on your site. From that it serves a `sitemap.xml` of every published entry, gives [menus](/verdin/guides/frontend/menus/) the paths of the entries they link to, and offers a ready-made `shared.seo` component for meta tags.

It is one of four site features, with [redirects](/verdin/guides/frontend/redirects/), [menus](/verdin/guides/frontend/menus/) and [forms](/verdin/guides/frontend/forms/). Strapi covers the same ground with community plugins (SEO, sitemap); in Verdin it is built in.

## Turn it on

[Section titled “Turn it on”](#turn-it-on)

1. In **Settings → Features**, turn on **SEO and sitemap**.
2. On its card, choose **Configure SEO**.
3. Enter the **Site URL**: the origin of your site, such as `https://www.example.com`. The sitemap’s URLs start with it.
4. Under **Content types**, give each type that has pages a **Path pattern**. Types without a pattern stay out of the sitemap. Optionally set a **Change frequency** and a **Priority** (0 to 1) for the sitemap.
5. Save, then choose **Open sitemap.xml** to check the result.

Changing the settings needs the **Manage features** permission (`features.manage`). See [Permissions](/verdin/reference/permissions/).

## Path patterns

[Section titled “Path patterns”](#path-patterns)

A pattern is a path that starts with `/`, with placeholders in braces:

| Pattern                 | Entry                           | Path                |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| `/blog/{slug}`          | Article with slug `hello-world` | `/blog/hello-world` |
| `/{locale}/blog/{slug}` | The French version of it        | `/fr/blog/bonjour`  |
| `/about`                | The Homepage single type        | `/about`            |

Placeholders are the type’s attributes (usually a `uid` such as `slug`) and `{locale}`. Values are URL-encoded. An entry whose placeholder is empty (a missing slug, say) has no path, and is left out of the sitemap and of menus. The dialog lists the attributes you can insert and refuses unknown ones.

The settings are stored as the feature’s settings, in this shape:

```json
{
  "baseUrl": "https://www.example.com",
  "types": {
    "api::article": { "pattern": "/{locale}/blog/{slug}", "changefreq": "weekly", "priority": 0.7 },
    "api::category": { "pattern": "/{locale}/topics/{slug}" }
  }
}
```

`changefreq` is one of `always`, `hourly`, `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, `yearly` or `never`.

## The sitemap

[Section titled “The sitemap”](#the-sitemap)

With a **Site URL** set, Verdin serves `/sitemap.xml` at the root of its own host (`https://cms.example.com/sitemap.xml`, outside the API prefix), with:

* every **published** entry of the configured types whose pattern fills;
* each entry’s last change (`lastmod`), and the type’s `changefreq` and `priority`;
* for localized types, one URL per locale, linked to each other with `<xhtml:link rel="alternate" hreflang="…">`;
* at most 50,000 URLs, the limit of a sitemap file.

```xml
<url>
  <loc>https://www.example.com/en/blog/hello-world</loc>
  <lastmod>2026-09-25T09:00:00.000Z</lastmod>
  <changefreq>weekly</changefreq>
  <priority>0.7</priority>
  <xhtml:link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href="https://www.example.com/en/blog/hello-world"/>
  <xhtml:link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="https://www.example.com/fr/blog/bonjour"/>
</url>
```

The sitemap is built at most every ten minutes and sent with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=600`, so a publish shows up within ten minutes.

Search engines expect the sitemap on your site’s host. Serve it from there with a rewrite or a small route that fetches Verdin’s:

Next.js: app/sitemap.xml/route.js

```js
export async function GET() {
  const response = await fetch('https://cms.example.com/sitemap.xml', { next: { revalidate: 600 } });
  return new Response(await response.text(), { headers: { 'content-type': 'application/xml' } });
}
```

Then list it in your `robots.txt`: `Sitemap: https://www.example.com/sitemap.xml`.

## The SEO component

[Section titled “The SEO component”](#the-seo-component)

Verdin suggests a `shared.seo` component with the fields of Strapi’s SEO plugin:

| Attribute         | Type                                    |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `metaTitle`       | string, required, at most 60 characters |
| `metaDescription` | text, required, at most 160 characters  |
| `metaImage`       | media (images)                          |
| `keywords`        | text                                    |
| `metaRobots`      | string                                  |
| `canonicalURL`    | string                                  |
| `structuredData`  | JSON                                    |

In the **Configure SEO** dialog, choose **Add the SEO component**, then **Create the component**. Creating it changes the schema, so the button is there in development mode (`verdin dev`) for admins with **Manage content types**; otherwise the dialog lists the attributes to add in your schema files instead. Then add a component field using `shared.seo` to each content type with pages, in the content-type builder.

Tip

With [AI actions](/verdin/guides/integrations/ai-actions/) on, a component that has `metaTitle` and `metaDescription` text attributes gets a **Suggest** button that fills them from the entry.

## Render the meta tags

[Section titled “Render the meta tags”](#render-the-meta-tags)

Populate the component and write the tags in your page’s head:

* REST

  Terminal

  ```sh
  curl -g 'https://cms.example.com/api/articles?filters[slug][$eq]=hello-world&populate[seo][populate]=*'
  ```

* GraphQL

  ```graphql
  query {
    articles(filters: { slug: { eq: "hello-world" } }) {
      title
      seo { metaTitle metaDescription metaRobots canonicalURL structuredData metaImage { url } }
    }
  }
  ```

* TypeScript

  ```ts
  const { data } = await verdin.collection('articles').find({
    filters: { slug: { $eq: 'hello-world' } },
    populate: { seo: { populate: '*' } },
  });
  const seo = data[0]?.seo;
  ```

```html
<title>{seo.metaTitle}</title>
<meta name="description" content="{seo.metaDescription}" />
<meta name="robots" content="{seo.metaRobots ?? 'index, follow'}" />
<link rel="canonical" href="{seo.canonicalURL ?? pageUrl}" />
<meta property="og:image" content="{cms + seo.metaImage.url}" />
<script type="application/ld+json">{JSON.stringify(seo.structuredData)}</script>
```

The example blog’s `shared.seo` has only `metaTitle` and `metaDescription`; the suggested component adds the rest. If the preview page uses [visual editing](/verdin/guides/frontend/visual-editing/), strip the invisible marks before measuring or comparing meta texts.

# Typed client

> Read and write Verdin content from TypeScript with @verdin/client and types generated from your schema by `verdin types`.

`@verdin/client` is a small TypeScript client for the content API: REST documents, the media library and GraphQL. Pair it with `verdin types`, which writes TypeScript definitions of your content types, and your editor checks route names, fields and write payloads as you type.

The client has no dependencies and runs anywhere `fetch` exists: browsers, Node 20 and later, Deno, Bun and edge workers. It is optional; every call maps to a plain HTTP request of the [REST API](/verdin/api/rest/).

## Install and generate types

[Section titled “Install and generate types”](#install-and-generate-types)

1. Install the package in your frontend project:

   Terminal

   ```sh
   npm install @verdin/client
   ```

2. In the Verdin project (the directory with `verdin.toml`), generate the types:

   Terminal

   ```sh
   verdin types -o ../site/src/verdin-types.ts
   ```

   Without `-o` (`--out`) the definitions go to standard output. The command only reads the schema files; it needs no database.

3. Create a client with the generated `VerdinSchema`:

   src/verdin.ts

   ```ts
   import { createClient } from '@verdin/client';
   import type { VerdinSchema } from './verdin-types';


   export const verdin = createClient<VerdinSchema>({
     url: 'https://cms.example.com',
     token: process.env.VERDIN_TOKEN, // omit to use the public role
   });
   ```

Run `verdin types` again after every schema change; the file says so in its first line. Committing it next to your frontend code, or regenerating it in CI, keeps both sides in step.

Caution

The token gives its holder the token’s permissions. Keep full-access and custom tokens on the server (SSR, build scripts, API routes). A browser bundle should use no token (the public role) or a read-only one. See [API tokens](/verdin/guides/auth/api-tokens/).

## What `verdin types` generates

[Section titled “What verdin types generates”](#what-verdin-types-generates)

For the [example blog](https://github.com/Verdin-CMS/verdin/blob/main/examples/blog/) (articles, categories, tags, a homepage single type and the `shared.seo`, `blocks.hero` and `blocks.quote` components) the file contains:

| Type                                           | What it is                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Article`, `Category`, `Tag`, `Homepage`       | One interface per content type, named after its `singularName`, extending `DocumentBase` (`id`, `documentId`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `publishedAt`). Private attributes are left out. |
| `ArticleInput`, …                              | The write types: every attribute optional, relations as `documentId` strings (or `connect` / `disconnect` / `set`), media as file ids, inverse relation sides left out.                  |
| `ComponentSharedSeo`, `ComponentBlocksHero`, … | One interface per component, plus its `…Input` type. Dynamic zone items carry a typed `__component`.                                                                                     |
| `Media`, `MediaFormat`, `Blocks`               | Media library files, their responsive formats and the rich text blocks format.                                                                                                           |
| `Collections`, `Singles`, `VerdinSchema`       | Routes (`articles`, `homepage`) mapped to their document and input types, for the client.                                                                                                |

Relations, media, components and dynamic zones are optional properties (`category?:`), because the API only returns them when you `populate` them. Big integers are `string`, since they do not fit JavaScript numbers.

Without the generated types the client still works: any route is accepted and documents are `Record<string, unknown>`.

## Read content

[Section titled “Read content”](#read-content)

* REST

  Terminal

  ```sh
  curl -g 'https://cms.example.com/api/articles?filters[title][$containsi]=rust&populate[category]=true&populate[seo]=true&sort[0]=publishedAt:desc&pagination[page]=1&pagination[pageSize]=10' \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $VERDIN_TOKEN"
  ```

* GraphQL

  ```graphql
  query {
    articles(
      filters: { title: { containsi: "rust" } }
      sort: ["publishedAt:desc"]
      pagination: { page: 1, pageSize: 10 }
    ) {
      documentId
      title
      slug
      category { name }
      seo { metaTitle metaDescription }
    }
  }
  ```

* TypeScript

  ```ts
  import { verdin } from './verdin';


  const { data, meta } = await verdin.collection('articles').find({
    filters: { title: { $containsi: 'rust' } },
    populate: { category: true, seo: true },
    sort: ['publishedAt:desc'],
    pagination: { page: 1, pageSize: 10 },
  });


  data[0].title; // string
  data[0].category?.name; // string | null | undefined
  meta.pagination.total;
  ```

Query parameters use Strapi v5’s format and are serialized in bracket notation, so any filter, sort, `fields`, `populate`, `status` or `locale` that works on the REST API works here. See [REST API](/verdin/api/rest/) for the full syntax.

| Call                                                                 | Request                                                                       |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `collection(route).find(params?)`                                    | `GET /api/:route`                                                             |
| `collection(route).findOne(documentId, params?)`                     | `GET /api/:route/:documentId`                                                 |
| `collection(route).create(data, params?)`                            | `POST /api/:route` (publishes unless `status: 'draft'`)                       |
| `collection(route).update(documentId, data, params?)`                | `PUT /api/:route/:documentId`                                                 |
| `collection(route).delete(documentId)`                               | `DELETE /api/:route/:documentId`                                              |
| `collection(route).publish(documentId)`, `unpublish`, `discardDraft` | `POST /api/:route/:documentId/actions/publish` (`unpublish`, `discard-draft`) |
| `single(route).find(params?)`, `update(data, params?)`, `delete()`   | `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE /api/:route`                                            |
| `upload(files, info?)`                                               | `POST /api/upload` (multipart)                                                |
| `files(params?)`                                                     | `GET /api/upload/files`                                                       |
| `graphql(query, variables?)`                                         | `POST /graphql`                                                               |

`stringify(params)` is exported too, for building query strings yourself (for example for a `<link rel="preload">`).

## Write content

[Section titled “Write content”](#write-content)

```ts
const { data: article } = await verdin.collection('articles').create(
  {
    title: 'Hello from TypeScript',
    category: 'hx2n8r3w0c1kq5v7m4j6b9a0',       // a category's documentId
    tags: { connect: ['t1…', 't2…'] },
    seo: { metaTitle: 'Hello', metaDescription: 'A first post' },
  },
  { status: 'draft' },
);


await verdin.collection('articles').publish(article.documentId);
```

Like in Strapi v5, `create` publishes the document right away on draft & publish types unless you pass `status: 'draft'`. Writes need a token with `create`, `update` or `publish` on the type; see [Permissions](/verdin/reference/permissions/).

Upload files with `upload`, then reference them by id:

```ts
const [cover] = await verdin.upload(file, { alternativeText: 'The team at the office' });
```

`file` is a `Blob` or `File` (or a list of them). Uploads need the `create` grant on the media library.

## GraphQL

[Section titled “GraphQL”](#graphql)

`graphql()` posts to `/graphql`, so the **GraphQL** feature must be on in **Settings → Features**. It returns the `data` of the response and throws on the first error.

```ts
const data = await verdin.graphql<{ articles: Array<{ title: string }> }>(
  `query ($q: String) { articles(filters: { title: { containsi: $q } }) { title } }`,
  { q: 'rust' },
);
```

The generated types describe the REST API. For GraphQL, pass the result type yourself, as above, or use a GraphQL code generator against the endpoint. See [GraphQL](/verdin/api/graphql/).

## Errors

[Section titled “Errors”](#errors)

Every failed request rejects with a `VerdinError`, carrying the error the API sent in Strapi’s format:

| Property  | Example                                                                                                     |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `status`  | `400`, `401`, `403`, `404`, `429`                                                                           |
| `name`    | `ValidationError`, `UnauthorizedError`, `ForbiddenError`, `NotFoundError`, `RateLimitError`, `GraphQLError` |
| `message` | A readable description.                                                                                     |
| `details` | The error’s details, such as the list of invalid fields of a `ValidationError`.                             |

```ts
import { VerdinError } from '@verdin/client';


try {
  const { data } = await verdin.collection('articles').findOne(id);
  return data;
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof VerdinError && error.status === 404) return null;
  throw error;
}
```

## Options

[Section titled “Options”](#options)

| Option    | Description                                                                                                             |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `url`     | The server origin, such as `https://cms.example.com`. Required.                                                         |
| `token`   | An API token or an end user’s JWT, sent as `Authorization: Bearer …`. Omit it for the public role.                      |
| `prefix`  | The content API prefix. Defaults to `/api`; match [`[api].prefix`](/verdin/reference/configuration/) if you changed it. |
| `fetch`   | A `fetch` implementation to use instead of the global one.                                                              |
| `headers` | Extra headers sent with every request.                                                                                  |

## Server rendering and edge runtimes

[Section titled “Server rendering and edge runtimes”](#server-rendering-and-edge-runtimes)

The client only calls `fetch`, so it runs unchanged in server components, API routes, build scripts and edge functions. Pass a custom `fetch` to add a framework’s cache options to every request. For example, with Next.js:

src/verdin.ts

```ts
export const verdin = createClient<VerdinSchema>({
  url: process.env.VERDIN_URL!,
  token: process.env.VERDIN_TOKEN,
  fetch: (input, init) => fetch(input, { ...init, next: { revalidate: 60, tags: ['verdin'] } }),
});
```

To read drafts on a preview page, send the preview token the admin put in the preview URL as a header:

```ts
const preview = createClient<VerdinSchema>({
  url: process.env.VERDIN_URL!,
  headers: { 'x-verdin-preview': searchParams.get('preview') ?? '' },
});
const { data } = await preview.collection('articles').findOne(id, { status: 'draft' });
```

See [Preview](/verdin/guides/content/preview/) for how preview links work, and [Visual editing](/verdin/guides/frontend/visual-editing/) to add click-to-edit to the same page.

Calling the API from a browser on another origin needs that origin in [`[api].cors_origins`](/verdin/reference/configuration/).

# Visual editing

> Let editors click text on your preview page and land on the field that holds it in the admin panel.

Visual editing turns your preview page into a map of the admin panel: an editor hovers a heading, clicks **Edit**, and the entry opens with that field focused. It builds on [Preview](/verdin/guides/content/preview/): set up preview URLs first, then add the two pieces below to the preview page.

Verdin hides a small, invisible source map in each text it returns (a technique known as *stega*), and an overlay script finds those texts on the page. Nothing changes in your components: the marked text renders like any other.

```
flowchart LR
A[Preview page] -- "x-verdin-stega: true" --> B[Content API]
B -- "text + invisible source map" --> A
A -- "visual-editing.js: click Edit" --> C[Admin panel field]
```

The page asks for source maps, and the overlay turns them into links to fields.

## Set it up

[Section titled “Set it up”](#set-it-up)

1. Turn on **Preview** in **Settings → Features**, choose **Configure preview URLs** and give each content type the URL of the page that renders it. The **Visual editing** section of the same dialog shows the script tag and header for your server. See [Preview](/verdin/guides/content/preview/).

2. On the preview page, fetch content with a token and the `x-verdin-stega: true` header. The token is the preview token from the preview URL (`?preview=…`, sent back as `x-verdin-preview`) or an API token:

   ```js
   const response = await fetch(`${CMS}/api/articles/${documentId}?status=draft&populate=*`, {
     headers: {
       'x-verdin-preview': previewToken, // or Authorization: Bearer <API token>
       'x-verdin-stega': 'true',
     },
   });
   ```

3. Load the overlay on the same page:

   ```html
   <script src="https://cms.example.com/admin/api/visual-editing.js" defer></script>
   ```

   The path follows [`[admin].path`](/verdin/reference/configuration/): `{path}/api/visual-editing.js`.

With the [typed client](/verdin/guides/frontend/typed-client/), pass both headers in `headers`:

```ts
const preview = createClient<VerdinSchema>({
  url: CMS,
  headers: { 'x-verdin-preview': previewToken, 'x-verdin-stega': 'true' },
});
const { data } = await preview.collection('articles').findOne(documentId, {
  status: 'draft',
  populate: '*',
});
```

Source maps are added to REST responses only, not to GraphQL: read preview content through the REST API.

Hover marked text on the page: it gets a green outline and an **Edit** button. Inside the admin’s side-by-side preview (**Open preview** → **Side by side**), the button asks the admin to open the field right there. When the page is open on its own, the button opens the entry in a new tab.

Note

Source maps are only added to `GET` requests that send `x-verdin-stega: true` **and** a token (`Authorization` or `x-verdin-preview`). Public traffic and anything your CDN caches never carry them, and marked responses are sent with `Cache-Control: private, no-store`.

## What gets marked

[Section titled “What gets marked”](#what-gets-marked)

| Marked                                                                           | Not marked                                |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `string`, `text` and `richtext` attributes                                       | `uid`, `email`, `password`, `enumeration` |
| The first text of each block of a `blocks` attribute                             | Numbers, booleans, dates, JSON            |
| The same inside components and dynamic zones (`seo.metaTitle`, `blocks.2.title`) | Empty strings                             |
| Populated relations, pointing at the related entry                               | Media fields                              |

The overlay also reads marks in `alt` and `title` attributes, so a marked text you put in one of them (a caption field used as `alt`, say) stays clickable.

## Strip marks where text is data

[Section titled “Strip marks where text is data”](#strip-marks-where-text-is-data)

The marks are invisible characters appended to the text. Where you use a value as data rather than show it (a key, a URL, a comparison, a `<title>` length check), strip them first:

```js
const clean = (text) => text.replace(/⁤[​-‍⁠]*⁣/g, '');


if (clean(article.category.name) === 'News') { /* … */ }
```

Fields that are data by nature, such as `uid` slugs and enumerations, are never marked, so routing on `slug` works as is.

## How a mark is encoded

[Section titled “How a mark is encoded”](#how-a-mark-is-encoded)

For tools that read the marks themselves: a mark is U+2064, then each UTF-8 byte of

```json
{"origin":"verdin","href":"https://cms.example.com/admin/content/api::article/<documentId>?locale=en&field=seo.metaTitle"}
```

as four base-4 digits (most significant first) written with U+200B, U+200C, U+200D and U+2060, then U+2063. The admin URL comes from [`[server].public_url`](/verdin/reference/configuration/) and `[admin].path`. The overlay sends `{ type: 'verdin:edit', href }` to the parent window with `postMessage`; the admin only acts on it when it comes from the preview URL’s origin.

# AI actions

> Give editors AI help in the admin panel (translation, alt text, summaries and SEO metadata) with the model provider you choose.

AI actions add four helpers to the admin panel: translate an entry from another locale, write alternative text for an image, summarize a long text into a short field, and suggest SEO metadata. They use a model provider you configure (Anthropic, OpenAI, or a local server such as Ollama), with your own key.

Every action returns a suggestion that fills the form. Nothing is saved until the editor reviews it and saves, and each action can be undone.

## Set it up

[Section titled “Set it up”](#set-it-up)

AI actions need both a provider in `verdin.toml` and the feature switched on.

1. Add an `[ai]` section and give the key to the server in `VERDIN_AI_KEY`:

   * Anthropic

     verdin.toml

     ```toml
     [ai]
     provider = "anthropic"
     # model = "claude-sonnet-5"   # the default
     ```

   * OpenAI

     verdin.toml

     ```toml
     [ai]
     provider = "openai"
     model = "gpt-4.1-mini"        # required: name the model you want
     ```

   * Local (Ollama)

     verdin.toml

     ```toml
     [ai]
     provider = "openai-compatible"
     base_url = "http://localhost:11434/v1"
     model = "llama3.2-vision"
     ```

     Local servers need no `VERDIN_AI_KEY`. LM Studio, vLLM and other servers with an OpenAI-compatible API work the same way.

   Terminal

   ```sh
   export VERDIN_AI_KEY=sk-...
   ```

2. Restart Verdin. It refuses to start when the section is incomplete: a missing key, or a missing `model` or `base_url` where the provider needs one.

3. In **Settings → Features**, turn on **AI actions**.

| Key          | Default                           | Description                                                                      |
| ------------ | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `provider`   | `"none"`                          | `anthropic`, `openai` or `openai-compatible`.                                    |
| `model`      | `claude-sonnet-5` for `anthropic` | The model. Required for the other providers.                                     |
| `base_url`   | The provider’s                    | Another endpoint: a proxy, or a local server (required for `openai-compatible`). |
| `max_tokens` | `2048`                            | Longest answer, in tokens.                                                       |

See [`[ai]`](/verdin/reference/configuration/). With the feature on but no `[ai]` section, the admin shows **AI actions are not available on this server.**

The alt text action sends images, so pick a model that accepts images if you want it.

## What the actions do

[Section titled “What the actions do”](#what-the-actions-do)

### Translate an entry

[Section titled “Translate an entry”](#translate-an-entry)

In the editor of a localized entry, **Translate from *locale*…** opens **Translate with AI**. Choose the locale to **Translate from** and choose **Translate**. The text fields of that locale’s saved draft (strings, texts, rich text, blocks, and the text inside components and dynamic zones) are translated into the current locale and replace those fields in the form.

* Fields shared between locales are left alone.
* Unsaved changes in the source locale are not included: save it first.
* Markdown, HTML, URLs, ids and block types are kept as they are.
* The translated fields are marked; review them, then save, or choose **Undo translation**.

This needs permission to update the entry in the target locale and to read it in the source locale.

### Write alternative text

[Section titled “Write alternative text”](#write-alternative-text)

In the media library, open an image and choose **Generate alt text**. The model describes the image (up to about 125 characters) in the default locale’s language, and fills the caption when it is empty. It works on JPEG, PNG, WebP and GIF images, and sends the `small` or `medium` format when there is one, so large originals are not uploaded to the provider. Needs the media library’s update permission (on the file, for **Own files**).

### Summarize into a field

[Section titled “Summarize into a field”](#summarize-into-a-field)

Text fields named like a summary (`description`, `summary`, `excerpt`, `abstract`, `intro`, `introduction`, `lead`, `teaser`) get a **Summarize *field*** button when the entry has a rich text or blocks field, or a text field named `body`, `content`, `text` or `article`. In the example blog, **Excerpt** gets **Summarize Body**. The summary fits the field’s maximum length.

### Suggest SEO metadata

[Section titled “Suggest SEO metadata”](#suggest-seo-metadata)

A component with `metaTitle` and `metaDescription` text attributes, such as the [suggested `shared.seo`](/verdin/guides/frontend/seo-and-sitemap/), gets a **Suggest** button. It fills the meta title, description and, when the component has one, `keywords`, from the entry’s saved draft.

## Limits

[Section titled “Limits”](#limits)

* Each admin may make 30 AI requests a minute; more answer **Too many AI requests. Wait a minute and try again.**
* Summaries and SEO suggestions send at most 40,000 characters of text.
* A request to the provider times out after 120 seconds.

## Privacy

[Section titled “Privacy”](#privacy)

Caution

AI actions send content to the provider you configure: the fields being translated, summarized or described, and the images for alt text. Choose a provider and a plan that your organization allows for that content, check its data retention terms, and consider a local model (`openai-compatible`) for content that must not leave your network.

* Requests go from the Verdin server to the provider; the key never reaches the browser.
* Only the action’s input is sent: the entry’s text fields, the text to summarize, or one image and its file name. Private attributes and other entries are not.
* Actions only read what the admin can already read, and suggestions are not stored.

The admin shows which model answered (**Suggestions by *model* (*provider*).**).

To let AI agents outside the admin read and write content, see [MCP server](/verdin/guides/integrations/mcp/).

# Deploys and CDN

> Give editors a Deploy button for your static site, track its builds, and purge your CDN when content changes.

Two tools for sites that cache what Verdin serves:

* **Deploys** put a **Deploy** button in the admin header. It calls your site’s build hook (Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages or any CI), and the provider reports back how the build goes.
* **CDN purges** tag content API responses by content type and purge those tags at Cloudflare, Fastly or your own endpoint when content changes publicly.

Both are part of the core: there is no feature switch. Deploys are set up in **Settings → Deployments**; the CDN in `verdin.toml`.

## Deploys

[Section titled “Deploys”](#deploys)

```
sequenceDiagram
participant E as Editor
participant V as Verdin
participant P as Build provider
E->>V: Deploy
V->>P: POST build hook
P-->>V: callback: building
P-->>V: callback: ready (url)
V-->>E: "Production site is deployed"
```

The Deploy button calls the build hook; the provider reports back to the callback URL.

### Add a target

[Section titled “Add a target”](#add-a-target)

1. At your provider, create a build hook for the site and copy its URL (Netlify: **Build hooks**; Vercel: **Deploy Hooks**; Cloudflare Pages: **Deploy hooks**; a CI: any URL that starts a pipeline on `POST`).
2. In Verdin, go to **Settings → Deployments** and choose **Add a target**.
3. Give it a **Name** (such as **Production site**) and paste the **Build hook URL**.
4. Save. The hook URL is a secret: from now on only its host is shown. To point the target at another hook, use **Replace URL**.

Admins who can deploy now see **Deploy** in the header. With several targets, it opens a **Deploy to** menu. After confirming, Verdin sends:

```http
POST <build hook URL>
content-type: application/json


{ "trigger": "verdin", "triggeredBy": "editor@example.com" }
```

A target deploys at most every 10 seconds, so a double click does not start two builds. The request times out after 15 seconds and does not follow redirects. A hook that answers with something other than `2xx` is recorded as **Refused**.

### Report build states back

[Section titled “Report build states back”](#report-build-states-back)

Without a callback, a deploy stays **Triggered**. To see **Building**, **Ready** and **Error** in the admin, and a link to the deployed site, give the provider the target’s callback URL: choose the target’s **Callback URL** button and copy it.

* Netlify

  In **Site configuration → Build & deploy → Deploy notifications**, add an outgoing webhook for **Deploy started**, **Deploy succeeded** and **Deploy failed**, with the callback URL.

* Vercel

  In **Team settings → Webhooks**, create a webhook for the `deployment.created`, `deployment.succeeded` and `deployment.error` events, with the callback URL.

* Other CI

  `POST` JSON with a `status` (`building`, `ready` or `error`) and, optionally, the deployed `url` and a `message`:

  Terminal

  ```sh
  curl -X POST "$VERDIN_CALLBACK_URL" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
    -d '{ "status": "ready", "url": "https://www.example.com" }'
  ```

Verdin understands Netlify’s `state`, Vercel’s `type` and a plain `status`, and updates the target’s latest deploy. It answers `204`, or `404` when the URL is wrong. The callback URL is `{public_url}{admin path}/api/deploy/callback/{id}/{secret}`, so set [`[server].public_url`](/verdin/reference/configuration/) to the address providers can reach.

Caution

The callback URL contains a secret: anyone who has it can report deploy states for that target. It cannot start deploys or read anything.

**Deploy history** lists the latest 50 deploys, newest first, with their target, start time, status, the hook’s HTTP status and the provider’s message. Deleting a target deletes its history, not the build hook.

### Permissions

[Section titled “Permissions”](#permissions)

| Permission                                              | Allows                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Trigger deploys** (`deploy.trigger`)                  | The **Deploy** button in the header. The built-in Editor role has it. |
| **Manage deploy targets and the CDN** (`deploy.manage`) | **Settings → Deployments**: targets, callback URLs and CDN purges.    |

See [Permissions](/verdin/reference/permissions/). Build hook URLs follow the same address rules as [webhooks](/verdin/guides/integrations/webhooks/): with `verdin start` they may not point at private networks unless [`[webhooks].allow_private_networks`](/verdin/reference/configuration/) allows it.

### Deploy on every change instead

[Section titled “Deploy on every change instead”](#deploy-on-every-change-instead)

The button suits sites that rebuild on demand. To rebuild on each publish, create a [webhook](/verdin/guides/integrations/webhooks/) for `entry.publish` and `entry.unpublish` with the build hook as its URL. For a scheduled batch of changes, publish them with a [release](/verdin/guides/content/releases/) and hook the webhook to `releases.publish`.

## CDN purges

[Section titled “CDN purges”](#cdn-purges)

When a CDN caches the content API, it serves stale content until the cache expires. With `[cdn]` set, Verdin tags its responses and purges the right tags as content changes, so you can cache for a long time.

### How tagging works

[Section titled “How tagging works”](#how-tagging-works)

Every successful `GET` of the content API carries `vd` (everything), `vd-<singularName>` (the content type) and the tag of every type its documents can populate: relation targets, also inside components and dynamic zones, followed to their own relations. For the blog example’s articles, in both header formats:

```http
Cache-Tag: vd,vd-article,vd-category,vd-tag
Surrogate-Key: vd vd-article vd-category vd-tag
```

A type with a polymorphic relation can reach any type, so its responses carry every type’s tag.

Cloudflare reads `Cache-Tag`, Fastly reads `Surrogate-Key`. When content changes publicly, Verdin purges the type’s tag:

* publishing, unpublishing or deleting an entry;
* any write to a type without draft & publish (its writes are public at once).

Saving a draft purges nothing, since drafts are not served publicly. Changes within a second (`debounce_ms`) are gathered into one purge, and a failed purge is retried twice.

### Configure it

[Section titled “Configure it”](#configure-it)

* Cloudflare

  verdin.toml

  ```toml
  [cdn]
  provider = "cloudflare"
  zone_id = "023e105f4ecef8ad9ca31a8372d0c353"
  ```

  `VERDIN_CDN_TOKEN` is an API token with the **Cache Purge** permission on the zone.

* Fastly

  verdin.toml

  ```toml
  [cdn]
  provider = "fastly"
  service_id = "SU1Z0isxPaozGVKXdv0eY"
  ```

  `VERDIN_CDN_TOKEN` is a Fastly API token allowed to purge the service.

* Webhook

  verdin.toml

  ```toml
  [cdn]
  provider = "webhook"
  url = "https://purge.example.com/verdin"
  ```

  Verdin sends `POST { "tags": ["vd-article"] }`, with `Authorization: Bearer <VERDIN_CDN_TOKEN>` when the token is set. Use it for another CDN, a reverse proxy or your framework’s revalidation API.

Terminal

```sh
export VERDIN_CDN_TOKEN=...
```

Verdin checks the section at start and refuses to run without the `zone_id`, `service_id`, `url` or token the provider needs. See [`[cdn]`](/verdin/reference/configuration/).

Your CDN still decides what to cache: set up a cache rule for the API paths (for example `/api/*` on anonymous `GET`s) with a long edge TTL. Keep authenticated requests, preview reads and `/api/_events` out of the cache.

### Check and purge by hand

[Section titled “Check and purge by hand”](#check-and-purge-by-hand)

The **CDN** section of **Settings → Deployments** shows the provider and **Recent purges** (**Purged** or **Failed**, with the tags). **Purge everything** drops every response tagged `vd`.

Because responses carry the tags of the types they can populate, renaming a category also purges the cached article lists that could include it, whether or not the request asked for `populate`.

Verdin’s own in-memory cache ([`[api].cache_ttl_secs`](/verdin/reference/configuration/)) is separate: it is emptied on every change.

# MCP server

> Let Claude and other AI agents read and edit Verdin content through the Model Context Protocol, with the permissions of an API token.

Verdin can serve its content to AI agents through the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) (MCP). Connect Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor or any other MCP client, and the agent can list your content types, query entries with the REST API’s filters, and create, update or publish entries, within the permissions of the token you give it.

Strapi v5 has no built-in MCP server.

## Turn it on

[Section titled “Turn it on”](#turn-it-on)
