4. Under **Collections**, open **Category**, select **New entry**, name it `News` and save.

5. Open **Article**, select **New entry**, and fill in a title, an excerpt and a body in Markdown. The `slug` is generated from the title. Pick `News` as the category and select **Publish**. Add a second article the same way.

6. Open **Settings → Public access**, allow **Find** and **Find one** for **Article** and **Category**, and select **Save**.

Check that the API answers:

Terminal

```sh
curl 'localhost:1337/api/articles?populate=category'
```

Note

Populating a relation needs read access to its target. Without **Find** on **Category**, `populate=category` answers `400` with ``invalid key `category` in populate``.

## 2. Create the Astro project

[Section titled “2. Create the Astro project”](#2-create-the-astro-project)

In a new terminal, next to `cms`:

Terminal

```sh
npm create astro@latest blog -- --template minimal --no-git --yes
cd blog
npm install @verdin/client marked
```

[`marked`](https://marked.js.org) turns the Markdown of the `body` field into HTML.

## 3. Generate the types

[Section titled “3. Generate the types”](#3-generate-the-types)

`verdin types` reads the schema and writes one TypeScript interface per content type and component, and a `VerdinSchema` map of routes for the client. Run it from `blog`, pointing at the Verdin project’s configuration:

Terminal

```sh
verdin types -c ../cms/verdin.toml -o src/verdin-types.ts
```

The file contains, among others:

src/verdin-types.ts

```ts
export interface Article extends DocumentBase {
  title: string;
  slug: string;
  excerpt: string | null;
  body: string | null;
  // …
  category?: Category | null;
  tags?: Tag[];
}
```

Relations, media and components are optional because the API returns them only when you populate them. Run the command again whenever the schema changes.

## 4. Connect to Verdin

[Section titled “4. Connect to Verdin”](#4-connect-to-verdin)

Declare the server’s URL, and an optional API token, in Astro’s typed environment:

astro.config.mjs

```js
// @ts-check
import { defineConfig, envField } from 'astro/config';


export default defineConfig({
  env: {
    schema: {
      VERDIN_URL: envField.string({ context: 'server', access: 'public', default: 'http://localhost:1337' }),
      VERDIN_TOKEN: envField.string({ context: 'server', access: 'secret', optional: true }),
    },
  },
});
```

Without a token the client reads as the public role, which is what you opened in step 1. To read with a token instead, create a **Read-only** one in **Settings → API tokens** and put it in `.env` as `VERDIN_TOKEN=…`.

Create the client once and share it:

src/lib/verdin.ts

```ts
import { createClient } from '@verdin/client';
import { VERDIN_TOKEN, VERDIN_URL } from 'astro:env/server';
import type { VerdinSchema } from '../verdin-types';


export const verdin = createClient<VerdinSchema>({
  url: VERDIN_URL,
  token: VERDIN_TOKEN,
});
```

`verdin.collection('articles')` now only accepts the routes of your schema, and its results are typed as `Article`.

## 5. Add a layout

[Section titled “5. Add a layout”](#5-add-a-layout)

Replace the starter page’s HTML with a layout the pages share:

src/layouts/Layout.astro

```astro
---
interface Props {
  title: string;
}


const { title } = Astro.props;
---


<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width" />
    <title>{title}</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <header><a href="/">My blog</a></header>
    <main>
      <slot />
    </main>
  </body>
</html>
```

## 6. List the articles

[Section titled “6. List the articles”](#6-list-the-articles)

src/pages/index.astro

```astro
---
import Layout from '../layouts/Layout.astro';
import { verdin } from '../lib/verdin';


const { data: articles } = await verdin.collection('articles').find({
  fields: ['title', 'slug', 'excerpt', 'publishedAt'],
  populate: { category: { fields: ['name'] } },
  sort: ['publishedAt:desc'],
});
---


<Layout title="My blog">
  <h1>Articles</h1>
  <ul>
    {articles.map((article) => (
      <li>
        <a href={`/articles/${article.slug}/`}>{article.title}</a>
        {article.category && <small> in {article.category.name}</small>}
        {article.excerpt && <p>{article.excerpt}</p>}
      </li>
    ))}
  </ul>
</Layout>
```

The query is the REST call `GET /api/articles?fields[0]=title&…&populate[category][fields][0]=name&sort[0]=publishedAt:desc`, in Strapi v5’s format. `fields` keeps the response small, and `populate` adds the category with only its name. The public role reads published articles only.

## 7. Add a page per article

[Section titled “7. Add a page per article”](#7-add-a-page-per-article)

Astro builds one page per article. `getStaticPaths` fetches the articles with their category and passes each one to its page:

src/pages/articles/\[slug].astro

```astro
---
import type { GetStaticPaths } from 'astro';
import { marked } from 'marked';
import Layout from '../../layouts/Layout.astro';
import { verdin } from '../../lib/verdin';


export const getStaticPaths = (async () => {
  const { data: articles } = await verdin.collection('articles').find({
    populate: { category: true },
    pagination: { pageSize: 100 },
  });
  return articles.map((article) => ({
    params: { slug: article.slug },
    props: { article },
  }));
}) satisfies GetStaticPaths;


const { article } = Astro.props;
const html = await marked.parse(article.body ?? '');
---


<Layout title={article.title}>
  <article>
    <h1>{article.title}</h1>
    {article.category && <p>Category: {article.category.name}</p>}
    <Fragment set:html={html} />
  </article>
</Layout>
```

`pageSize` is capped by `[api].max_page_size` (100 by default). With more articles, fetch the pages in a loop using `meta.pagination.pageCount`.

Caution

`marked` does not sanitize HTML. That is fine for Markdown your own editors write; if the content can come from untrusted people, sanitize the HTML before rendering it.

## 8. Run it

[Section titled “8. Run it”](#8-run-it)

Terminal

```sh
npm run dev
```

Open <http://localhost:4321>: the list shows your published articles, and each links to its page. `npm run build` writes the static site to `dist/`.

A static build reads the content once. To publish changes, rebuild the site when content changes, for example from a webhook or a deploy hook; see [Deploys and CDN](/verdin/guides/integrations/deploys-and-cdn/).

Your project now looks like this:

* blog/

  * astro.config.mjs

  * src/

    * verdin-types.ts generated by `verdin types`

    * lib/

      * verdin.ts

    * layouts/

      * Layout.astro

    * pages/

      * index.astro

      * articles/

        * \[slug].astro

## 9. Optional: preview drafts

[Section titled “9. Optional: preview drafts”](#9-optional-preview-drafts)

The admin can open a draft on your site with a short-lived preview token. The token reads that one document, drafts included, and nothing else. Because drafts change after the build, the preview page renders on each request, which needs an adapter:

Terminal

```sh
npx astro add node --yes
```

Add a client that sends the preview token in the `x-verdin-preview` header:

src/lib/verdin.ts

```diff
import { createClient } from '@verdin/client';
import { VERDIN_TOKEN, VERDIN_URL } from 'astro:env/server';
import type { VerdinSchema } from '../verdin-types';


export const verdin = createClient<VerdinSchema>({
  url: VERDIN_URL,
  token: VERDIN_TOKEN,
});


+/** A client that reads one draft with the preview token from the admin's link. */
+export function previewClient(previewToken: string) {
  +return createClient<VerdinSchema>({
+    url: VERDIN_URL,
+    headers: { 'x-verdin-preview': previewToken },
+  });
+}
```

Then the page. `prerender = false` renders it on demand; the token arrives as the `preview` query parameter:

src/pages/preview/\[documentId].astro

```astro
---
import { VerdinError } from '@verdin/client';
import { marked } from 'marked';
import Layout from '../../layouts/Layout.astro';
import { previewClient } from '../../lib/verdin';


export const prerender = false;


const { documentId } = Astro.params;
const token = Astro.url.searchParams.get('preview');
if (!documentId || !token) {
  return new Response('Missing preview token', { status: 401 });
}


let article;
try {
  ({ data: article } = await previewClient(token)
    .collection('articles')
    .findOne(documentId, { status: 'draft', populate: { category: true } }));
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof VerdinError) {
    return new Response('This preview link has expired', { status: error.status });
  }
  throw error;
}
const html = await marked.parse(article.body ?? '');
Astro.response.headers.set('cache-control', 'no-store');
---


<Layout title={`Preview: ${article.title}`}>
  <p><strong>Draft preview</strong></p>
  <article>
    <h1>{article.title}</h1>
    {article.category && <p>Category: {article.category.name}</p>}
    <Fragment set:html={html} />
  </article>
</Layout>
```

A preview token cannot list entries, so the page looks the draft up by `documentId` rather than by slug. Now tell Verdin where the page is:

1. In the admin, open **Settings → Features**, turn on **Preview** and select **Configure preview URLs**.
2. Set the URL template of **Article** to `http://localhost:4321/preview/{documentId}` and save. Verdin appends the token as `?preview=…`.
3. Open an article, change it and select **Save draft**, then select **Open preview**.

The page shows the draft. Links last 60 minutes by default. See [Preview](/verdin/guides/content/preview/) for the placeholders and settings, and [Visual editing](/verdin/guides/frontend/visual-editing/) to edit from the preview.

## Next steps

[Section titled “Next steps”](#next-steps)

* [Typed client](/verdin/guides/frontend/typed-client/): every method of `@verdin/client`.
* [REST API](/verdin/api/rest/): filters, sorting, pagination and `populate`.
* [Images](/verdin/guides/frontend/images/): responsive formats of the media library.
* [SEO and sitemap](/verdin/guides/frontend/seo-and-sitemap/): the `shared.seo` component and Verdin’s sitemap.

# Tutorial: a blog with Next.js

> Build a small Next.js App Router blog on Verdin's example schema, with typed queries, article pages by slug, categories and an optional draft preview.

In this tutorial you build a blog with [Next.js](https://nextjs.org) and the App Router that reads its content from Verdin: a home page that lists articles, one page per article at `/articles/<slug>` with its category, and, optionally, a page that shows drafts from the admin’s preview link. You use the typed client `@verdin/client` with types generated from the schema, in Server Components.

Written for Next.js 16.3 (`create-next-app` 16.3), React 19.2 and Node.js 20.9 or later, with Verdin and `@verdin/client` 0.10. It uses Next.js’s default caching, without `cacheComponents`. The [Astro tutorial](/verdin/start/tutorial-astro/) builds the same blog with Astro.

## Before you start

[Section titled “Before you start”](#before-you-start)

You need the `verdin` binary on your `PATH` (see the [Quickstart](/verdin/start/quickstart/)), Node.js and Git. You end up with two folders side by side: `cms`, the Verdin project, and `blog`, the Next.js app.

## 1. Set up Verdin with the blog schema

[Section titled “1. Set up Verdin with the blog schema”](#1-set-up-verdin-with-the-blog-schema)

The repository’s [`examples/blog`](https://github.com/Verdin-CMS/verdin/tree/main/examples/blog) project models a blog: articles with a title, a `slug`, an excerpt, a Markdown `body`, a category and tags, plus a homepage single type and a few components.

1. Create a Verdin project and copy the example schema into it:

   Terminal

   ```sh
   git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/Verdin-CMS/verdin.git
   verdin new cms
   cp verdin/examples/blog/schema/content-types/{article,category,tag,homepage}.json cms/schema/content-types/
   cp -r verdin/examples/blog/schema/components/* cms/schema/components/
   ```

2. Start it:

   Terminal

   ```sh
   cd cms
   verdin dev
   ```

   The first start creates the tables for the four content types.

3. Open <http://localhost:1337/admin/> and create the first admin.

4. Under **Collections**, open **Category**, select **New entry**, name it `News` and save.

5. Open **Article**, select **New entry**, and fill in a title, an excerpt and a body in Markdown. The `slug` is generated from the title. Pick `News` as the category and select **Publish**. Add a second article the same way.

6. Open **Settings → Public access**, allow **Find** and **Find one** for **Article** and **Category**, and select **Save**.

Check that the API answers:

Terminal

```sh
curl 'localhost:1337/api/articles?populate=category'
```

Note

Populating a relation needs read access to its target. Without **Find** on **Category**, `populate=category` answers `400` with ``invalid key `category` in populate``.

## 2. Create the Next.js app

[Section titled “2. Create the Next.js app”](#2-create-the-nextjs-app)

In a new terminal, next to `cms`:

Terminal

```sh
npx create-next-app@latest blog --ts --app --src-dir --no-tailwind --no-eslint --no-react-compiler --import-alias '@/*' --yes
cd blog
npm install @verdin/client marked
```

[`marked`](https://marked.js.org) turns the Markdown of the `body` field into HTML.

## 3. Generate the types

[Section titled “3. Generate the types”](#3-generate-the-types)

`verdin types` reads the schema and writes one TypeScript interface per content type and component, and a `VerdinSchema` map of routes for the client. Run it from `blog`, pointing at the Verdin project’s configuration:

Terminal

```sh
verdin types -c ../cms/verdin.toml -o src/verdin-types.ts
```

The file contains, among others:

src/verdin-types.ts

```ts
export interface Article extends DocumentBase {
  title: string;
  slug: string;
  excerpt: string | null;
  body: string | null;
  // …
  category?: Category | null;
  tags?: Tag[];
}
```

Relations, media and components are optional because the API returns them only when you populate them. Run the command again whenever the schema changes.

## 4. Connect to Verdin

[Section titled “4. Connect to Verdin”](#4-connect-to-verdin)

Put the server’s URL in `.env.local`:

.env.local

```sh
VERDIN_URL=http://localhost:1337
# VERDIN_TOKEN=…
```

Without a token the client reads as the public role, which is what you opened in step 1. To read with a token instead, create a **Read-only** one in **Settings → API tokens** and set `VERDIN_TOKEN`. Both variables stay on the server: they have no `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix, and the client only runs in Server Components.

Create the client once and share it:

src/lib/verdin.ts

```ts
import { createClient } from '@verdin/client';
import type { VerdinSchema } from '@/verdin-types';


const url = process.env.VERDIN_URL ?? 'http://localhost:1337';


export const verdin = createClient<VerdinSchema>({
  url,
  token: process.env.VERDIN_TOKEN,
});
```

`verdin.collection('articles')` now only accepts the routes of your schema, and its results are typed as `Article`.

## 5. Replace the layout

[Section titled “5. Replace the layout”](#5-replace-the-layout)

Replace the starter layout, and delete `src/app/page.module.css`, which the new pages do not use:

src/app/layout.tsx

```tsx
import type { Metadata } from 'next';
import Link from 'next/link';


export const metadata: Metadata = {
  title: 'My blog',
};


export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <header>
          <Link href="/">My blog</Link>
        </header>
        <main>{children}</main>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

## 6. List the articles

[Section titled “6. List the articles”](#6-list-the-articles)

src/app/page.tsx

```tsx
import Link from 'next/link';
import { verdin } from '@/lib/verdin';


export const revalidate = 60;


export default async function Home() {
  const { data: articles } = await verdin.collection('articles').find({
    fields: ['title', 'slug', 'excerpt', 'publishedAt'],
    populate: { category: { fields: ['name'] } },
    sort: ['publishedAt:desc'],
  });


  return (
    <>
      <h1>Articles</h1>
      <ul>
        {articles.map((article) => (
          <li key={article.documentId}>
            <Link href={`/articles/${article.slug}`}>{article.title}</Link>
            {article.category && <small> in {article.category.name}</small>}
            {article.excerpt && <p>{article.excerpt}</p>}
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </>
  );
}
```

The query is the REST call `GET /api/articles?fields[0]=title&…&populate[category][fields][0]=name&sort[0]=publishedAt:desc`, in Strapi v5’s format. `fields` keeps the response small, and `populate` adds the category with only its name. The public role reads published articles only.

`revalidate = 60` prerenders the page at build time and refreshes it at most once a minute after that, so published changes show up without a rebuild.

## 7. Add a page per article

[Section titled “7. Add a page per article”](#7-add-a-page-per-article)

The article page finds its article by slug with a filter. `generateStaticParams` prerenders the existing articles; articles published later render on their first visit.

src/app/articles/\[slug]/page.tsx

```tsx
import type { Metadata } from 'next';
import { notFound } from 'next/navigation';
import { marked } from 'marked';
import { verdin } from '@/lib/verdin';


export const revalidate = 60;


type Props = { params: Promise<{ slug: string }> };


async function getArticle(slug: string) {
  const { data } = await verdin.collection('articles').find({
    filters: { slug: { $eq: slug } },
    populate: { category: true },
    pagination: { pageSize: 1 },
  });
  return data[0];
}


export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const { data: articles } = await verdin.collection('articles').find({
    fields: ['slug'],
    pagination: { pageSize: 100 },
  });
  return articles.map((article) => ({ slug: article.slug }));
}


export async function generateMetadata({ params }: Props): Promise<Metadata> {
  const article = await getArticle((await params).slug);
  return { title: article?.title };
}


export default async function ArticlePage({ params }: Props) {
  const article = await getArticle((await params).slug);
  if (!article) notFound();
  const html = await marked.parse(article.body ?? '');


  return (
    <article>
      <h1>{article.title}</h1>
      {article.category && <p>Category: {article.category.name}</p>}
      <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: html }} />
    </article>
  );
}
```

In Next.js 16, `params` is a promise: await it before reading the slug. An unknown slug finds no article and answers 404 through `notFound()`. `pageSize` is capped by `[api].max_page_size` (100 by default).

Caution

`marked` does not sanitize HTML. That is fine for Markdown your own editors write; if the content can come from untrusted people, sanitize the HTML before rendering it.

## 8. Run it

[Section titled “8. Run it”](#8-run-it)

Terminal

```sh
npm run dev
```

Open <http://localhost:3000>: the list shows your published articles, and each links to its page. `npm run build` needs Verdin running, because it fetches the articles to prerender them.

To refresh pages as soon as content changes instead of within a minute, call `revalidatePath` from a route handler that a Verdin webhook triggers; see [Webhooks](/verdin/guides/integrations/webhooks/).

Your project now looks like this:

* blog/

  * .env.local

  * src/

    * verdin-types.ts generated by `verdin types`

    * lib/

      * verdin.ts

    * app/

      * layout.tsx

      * page.tsx

      * articles/

        * \[slug]/

          * page.tsx

## 9. Optional: preview drafts

[Section titled “9. Optional: preview drafts”](#9-optional-preview-drafts)

The admin can open a draft on your site with a short-lived preview token. The token reads that one document, drafts included, and nothing else.

Add a client that sends the preview token in the `x-verdin-preview` header:

src/lib/verdin.ts

```diff
import { createClient } from '@verdin/client';
import type { VerdinSchema } from '@/verdin-types';


const url = process.env.VERDIN_URL ?? 'http://localhost:1337';


export const verdin = createClient<VerdinSchema>({
  url,
  token: process.env.VERDIN_TOKEN,
});


+/** A client that reads one draft with the preview token from the admin's link. */
+export function previewClient(previewToken: string) {
  +return createClient<VerdinSchema>({
+    url,
+    headers: { 'x-verdin-preview': previewToken },
+  });
+}
```

Then the page. It reads `searchParams`, so Next.js renders it on each request; the token arrives as the `preview` query parameter:

src/app/preview/\[documentId]/page.tsx

```tsx
import { VerdinError } from '@verdin/client';
import { notFound } from 'next/navigation';
import { marked } from 'marked';
import { previewClient } from '@/lib/verdin';


type Props = {
  params: Promise<{ documentId: string }>;
  searchParams: Promise<{ preview?: string }>;
};


export default async function PreviewPage({ params, searchParams }: Props) {
  const { documentId } = await params;
  const { preview } = await searchParams;
  if (!preview) notFound();


  let article;
  try {
    ({ data: article } = await previewClient(preview)
      .collection('articles')
      .findOne(documentId, { status: 'draft', populate: { category: true } }));
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof VerdinError) {
      return <p>This preview link is invalid or has expired.</p>;
    }
    throw error;
  }
  const html = await marked.parse(article.body ?? '');


  return (
    <article>
      <p>
        <strong>Draft preview</strong>
      </p>
      <h1>{article.title}</h1>
      {article.category && <p>Category: {article.category.name}</p>}
      <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: html }} />
    </article>
  );
}
```

A preview token cannot list entries, so the page looks the draft up by `documentId` rather than by slug. Now tell Verdin where the page is:

1. In the admin, open **Settings → Features**, turn on **Preview** and select **Configure preview URLs**.
2. Set the URL template of **Article** to `http://localhost:3000/preview/{documentId}` and save. Verdin appends the token as `?preview=…`.
3. Open an article, change it and select **Save draft**, then select **Open preview**.

The page shows the draft. Links last 60 minutes by default. See [Preview](/verdin/guides/content/preview/) for the placeholders and settings, and [Visual editing](/verdin/guides/frontend/visual-editing/) to edit from the preview.
